On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Sitaram is the loyal guard standing in Udayaditya's way: though he respects the prince and owes him his life twice, he refuses to open the locked door at swordpoint, choosing duty over defiance, and must be disarmed and bound by Udayaditya to escape the king's punishment. On the night of Udayaditya's own escape, the roles invert — Sitaram becomes the rescuer, rushing into the burning prison to carry the passive, confined Udayaditya out to freedom. The man who once had to be overpowered to let Udayaditya out now risks everything to let Udayaditya out himself, repaying the debt of the two lives Udayaditya had saved, while Udayaditya shifts from sword-wielding actor to helpless beneficiary of another's loyalty.

The initial plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; it failed because one Pathan refused to carry out the murder. The successful method was sending Muktiyar Khan with soldiers to Raigarh, where Abdul executed Basanta Ray with a sword.
In the inner quarters of the Jessore palace, disguised as a middle-aged woman; and in the king's chamber at Chandradwip, in his own guise as the jester.

Rukmini, living in disguise as the widow Mangala, prepares a poison over five days, chanting mantras and performing rituals to ensure the Yubaraj feels no pity when Surma dies. The Mahishi, seeking to win Udayaditya's heart back from Surma, sends Matangini to secretly fetch "medicine" from Mangala. Surma takes the poison, falls gravely ill, and dies at dawn before she can be exiled.
Ramchandra Ray, his honor wounded by Vibha's refusal, decides to take another wife, causing Vibha to lose her place in her husband's household and arrive too late to reclaim it.

Rukmini obtained the ring from Udayaditya during her nighttime visit, then passed it to Sitaram and Bhagavat. They used its seal to stamp a forged petition, purportedly from the Yubaraj, accusing Pratapaditya of treason. Bhagavat delivered this petition to Pratapaditya as supposed intercepted evidence, which led directly to Udayaditya's imprisonment.

The escape enrages Pratapaditya, who then notices Udayaditya's monthly stipends to the dismissed guards Sitaram and Bhagavat. When Pratapaditya forbids this charity, Surma secretly continues it through a maid. When word of the secret stipends reaches Pratapaditya, he orders Surma to her paternal home.

The song expresses the anguish of outliving one's loved ones—those once his no longer answer his call, leaving only emptiness. Basanta Ray first sings it alone in Raigarh at sunset, spontaneously voicing his private grief for the family he has lost. He then sings it again in Jessore, this time to Vibha, after seeing the silent, empty room and confirming that Udayaditya is truly imprisoned—transforming the song from solitary lament into a shared expression of the family's ruin.

Rukmini's failure to stop the escape leaves her enraged and desperate for revenge. She goes directly to Pratapaditya and reveals that the old king of Raigarh (Basanta Ray) conspired with Sitaram to steal Udayaditya away. This disclosure enrages Pratapaditya, who then secretly dispatches the Pathan commander Muktiyar Khan with a signed death order for the King of Raigarh. Muktiyar Khan captures Udayaditya, then enters the fort in plain clothes and carries out the order, resulting in Basanta Ray's execution. Thus Rukmini's failed physical intervention leads her to expose Basanta Ray's role to the king, which triggers the death sentence.

Pratapaditya's reception of Ramchandra Ray is cold and deliberately dismissive—he provides no musical fanfare, sends a modest welcome party, and treats Ramchandra with calm indifference, interrupting him to attend to state business before dismissing him. This silent superiority wounds Ramchandra's pride deeply. In contrast, Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya's status in his own court through open mockery and ridicule—laughing as courtiers and Ramai Bhand belittle Pratapaditya's lineage and character, and taking daily pleasure in verbal attacks against him. Where Pratapaditya's slight is restrained and dignified, Ramchandra's response is petty and vindictive, attempting to compensate for his humiliation by tearing Pratapaditya down with words rather than silent authority.

The widow, Rukmini, re-enters Udayaditya's life under the name Mangala, living on the outskirts of Jessore. She schemes to win him back, using manipulation and poison to eliminate Surma, whose death brings tragedy to the royal household of Jessore.

Udayaditya's early lament—that he wished he had never been born the crown prince, that he was unfit to rule, and that his father's neglect proved it—culminates in a formal, sworn renunciation. After being brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he declares he does not want the kingdom and pleads for release from the throne. To prove his sincerity, he swears a solemn oath before Ma-Kali that he will never accept even an iota of the kingdom, never sit on its throne, nor touch its scepter, naming Samaraditya as heir instead. He then asks only for money to establish a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name and departs for Kashi as an ascetic—transforming his childhood wish to escape the crown into a binding, lifelong renunciation.

Nayanchand, fearful of Pratapaditya's reaction, intercepts the letter and delivers it to the Mahishi instead of the Maharaj. After Basanta Ray reads it, he advises the Mahishi to announce throughout the household that Ramchandra has written requesting Vibha's return to Chandradwip—a complete misrepresentation of the letter's actual contents, in which Ramchandra renounces Vibha and declares she should not be sent. The Mahishi then tells Vibha this false version, and Vibha, believing her husband has forgiven her and sent for her, is filled with joy.

Pratapaditya ordered the canal adjoining the palace blocked with large Sal wood logs, knowing Ramchandra Ray's boat was moored there. The trap failed in two ways: once Ramchandra was lowered into the boat, Rammohan and his followers simply pulled the boat up and over the logs, and when the guards ran to fetch a boat to give chase, the man sent for it stopped at Harimudi's shop for a pipe of tobacco and to press Ramashankar for a debt, delaying the pursuit so long that catching the boat became impossible. The boat thus got through to the Bhairav river, where Fernandez fired a cannon.

The sitar symbolizes Basanta Ray's capacity for joy and his bond with his loved ones, so its decline mirrors his deepening despair. When he decides to leave, he abandons the sitar entirely, declaring he will no longer play it — music has lost its meaning without those he loves. Later, when asked about it, he explains that the sitar remains but its strings have broken and can no longer be tuned, an image of his own inner state: grief has rendered him unable to produce the music that once came naturally. Even his attempt to play before leaving is frustrated by tears, forcing him to set the instrument down. Only when Khan Saheb sings for him does the music return, and then it is another's voice, not his own — underscoring that his personal source of joy has been silenced by the loss and suffering surrounding Udayaditya.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for courageously involving himself in the affairs of the subjects and would intervene to protect them from oppression without considering the consequences. After Surma's death, a blind fear of Pratapaditya took hold of him; he became hesitant and withdrawn, no longer daring to act against injustice—when he witnessed a subject being beaten, he fled indoors instead of stopping the official, and he failed to send aid to those in need, paralyzed by the belief that his fate was entirely in Pratapaditya's hands.

Sitaram undoes the damage by helping Udayaditya escape from prison. During a fire that breaks out near the palace, Sitaram enters Udayaditya's prison cell, tells him the prison is on fire, and helps him flee to safety in a nearby field.

On the first occasion, at Pratapaditya's palace in Jessore, Rammohan fashions a rope by twisting together thick sheets, ties it to a roof pillar, climbs down with Ramchandra Ray on his back, then grips the rope with his teeth to free both hands and lowers Ramchandra into the waiting boat before jumping down himself. On the second occasion, after Vibha faints from being publicly insulted, Rammohan lifts her and carries her out of the palace, places her in a palanquin at the gate, and takes her back to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is adorned as a royal bride: eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate coiffure—all imposed by the Mahishi against her own taste (she had wanted only three thin turquoise bangles), leaving her flustered yet radiant with joy. In Chandradwip, she deliberately goes "like a common subject, like a beggar-woman," rejecting a palanquin, her veil fallen, entering the palace unrecognized "like any other maidservant"—her presentation stripped of all ornament and status, mirroring her fall from a joyous bride-to-be to a humiliated woman surrendering herself at the king's feet.

In his bedchamber, the window symbolizes Udayaditya's longing and hope for Surma's return—he sits there gazing at the same moonlight and garden, unable to accept that she is gone, leaving her spot empty as if she might still appear. In the prison cell, the window transforms into a symbol of freedom and hope for liberation—through it he sees the sky and flying birds, which remind him that his cage will one day break and he will be free; it becomes the one small patch of land where he feels naturally free, no king or emperor able to hold him captive. The window shifts from a site of grief and memory to a site of spiritual and physical liberation.

Their relationship deteriorates through three stages. Initially, Sitaram borrows money from Rukmini, and their exchanges are flirtatious—he calls her "Pranpriye" and she feigns affection while lending him cash. The dynamic turns hostile when Sitaram, enraged by Udayaditya's imprisonment, storms into Rukmini's house, curses her, and threatens to burn her home and grind her face on stone. Rukmini nearly attacks him in return, claiming Udayaditya is hers to protect. The final stage becomes life-threatening when Sitaram, having set the prison fire to help Udayaditya escape, goes to Rukmini's house intending to steal her money, believing her dead. He finds her alive, disheveled, and enraged, declaring she has returned from the door of Yama and will kill him. She grabs a curved blade and chases him; Sitaram flees for his life, realizing too late that he should have strangled her when he had the chance.

The fire begins as a simple distraction: it draws the guards away from Udayaditya's door, allowing Sitaram to enter and escort him out. Sitaram's men then escalate the chaos by actively sabotaging firefighting efforts—pouring water in the wrong places, breaking pots, and creating confusion—ensuring the blaze continues and no one notices the empty cell. Once Udayaditya is gone, Sitaram's men set his cell ablaze themselves, transforming the scene from a rescue into a staged death. Sitaram plants false evidence by throwing bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the burning room to suggest he perished there. He then spreads the rumor that the Yubaraj died in the fire, claiming the roof collapsed and no response came from inside. Witnesses emerge—some claiming they saw him through the window, others that they heard screams, and one producing the burnt sword remains—lending credibility to the deception. The strategy culminates in Pratapaditya initially accepting the death narrative, though the truth later surfaces through a fisherman's report and other sources.

Ramchandra Ray was not grateful that Udayaditya had saved his life. He felt it was bound to happen—that if he were in peril, everyone would unite to save him. He believed Udayaditya had saved him for the sake of his own sister, Vibha, and that saving his life had not been Udayaditya's main objective. For the crime of being Pratapaditya's son, Ramchandra Ray brought up his name in court and laughed and joked without a care.

Pratapaditya openly scorned the minister's warnings, declaring the Emperor of Delhi was not his God and forbidding even the mention of his name. That dismissed threat was then turned into a weapon by Bhagavat and Sitaram: they forged a petition bearing Prince Udayaditya's seal, making it appear the son had lodged a treason complaint against Pratapaditya with the Emperor of Delhi to seize the kingdom for himself. By delivering this intercepted petition to the king, they transformed the Emperor's authority—the very power Pratapaditya had mocked—into the instrument used to move against his own son.

In Chapter 8, Vibha's hair becomes a site of contention: the Mahishi imposes her own styling, but Vibha secretly has Surma redo it to her own liking, marking Surma's touch as one of affection and personal understanding. After Surma's absence, in Chapter 18, Vibha sits quietly at braiding time as if Surma will come to braid it for her, but her hair remains unbraided—a daily, physical reminder that Surma is gone. By Chapter 23, Rammohan explicitly notes Vibha's unkempt hair as a visible sign of her sorrow and neglect. Thus Vibha's hair traces Surma's presence through intimate care and her absence through its unbraided, neglected state.
